2027-06-26.title: Saturday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The Lord has remembered his mercy
Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word
2027-06-26.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). The responsorial psalm is Mary's canticle, the Magnificat. As on other Saturdays in Ordinary Time with no obligatory memorial, the optional memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may be celebrated. Liturgical colour: green (white if the Saturday memorial of Mary is kept).
2027-06-26.verse: The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.”
theo: It is the hottest hour of the day at the oaks of Mamre, near Hebron. Old Abraham is sitting at the entrance of his tent, the time when no sensible traveller is on the road. “He looked up and saw three men standing near him.” What follows is the most famous picture of hospitality in the Bible, and it is full of movement: Abraham “ran from the tent entrance to meet them,” bowed to the ground, “hastened into the tent to Sarah,” “ran to the herd.” A man of ninety-nine is running. He offers “a little water” and “a little bread” and then lays out a feast: cakes from three measures of choice flour, a calf “tender and good,” curds and milk, and he himself stands by them under the tree while they eat, like a servant. The narrator has already told us the secret that Abraham does not yet know: “The LORD appeared to Abraham.” In welcoming three strangers, he is welcoming God. The Letter to the Hebrews remembers this scene: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). Many Fathers of the Church saw in the three visitors, addressed now as “my lord” and now as “they,” a first shadow of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and the famous Russian icon of Andrei Rublev paints them at Abraham's table. Then the guests ask, “Where is your wife Sarah?” and the promise is repeated, this time in her hearing: “your wife Sarah shall have a son.” Sarah, listening behind the tent flap, laughs to herself, as Abraham had laughed. And the Lord asks the question that runs through the whole Bible: “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?” Sarah, afraid, denies it: “I did not laugh.” God answers gently and firmly: “Oh yes, you did laugh.” God is not offended by her laugh; he simply will not let her pretend.

Today's psalm is the song of another woman who received a promise that seemed impossible. To Mary in Nazareth the angel Gabriel used almost the same words that were spoken at Mamre: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). Sarah laughed and hid; Mary asked her question and then said yes. And her Magnificat ends by reaching back to this very tent: God has helped his servant Israel, “according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.” On Saturdays the Church likes to honour Mary, and the readings give us good reason today. In the Gospel Jesus enters Capernaum and meets a Roman centurion, an officer of the occupying army, a Gentile. He asks for help for his paralysed servant. Jesus offers to come, and the centurion answers with words that the Church has placed on our lips before every Communion: “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.” He knows that Jesus' word is enough, as a soldier's command is enough. Jesus is amazed and promises that “many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” Abraham's table at Mamre has become a table for all nations. The warning that follows, that “the heirs of the kingdom” may be left outside, is addressed to anyone who presumes on God's gifts; it is not a judgment on the Jewish people (Catechism 597–598), and it speaks first of all to us who are already at the table. Then Jesus enters Peter's house and touches the hand of his mother-in-law; the fever leaves her, “and she got up and began to serve him.” By evening he heals all who are brought to him, and Matthew sees the Servant of Isaiah at work: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.”
outline: Ask: when did a visitor to your home turn out to be a blessing you did not expect?
At Mamre, welcoming strangers means welcoming God.
Point 2 · Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
Sarah laughs and hides; Mary believes and sings.
The centurion's faith, a table for all nations, and a healed woman who serves.
“Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?”
live: Invite someone to your table this week, or welcome an unexpected visitor with a little water and a little bread, as Abraham did.
At your next Communion, say Lord, I am not worthy slowly and with faith, thinking of one person you are carrying to Jesus, as the centurion carried his servant.
2027-06-26.prayer: Lord God, you came to Abraham at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and he ran to welcome you. Teach us to see you in the stranger and the guest. When we laugh at your promises or hide our doubts, ask us again: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? Give us the faith of Mary, who believed that nothing is impossible with you, and the faith of the centurion, who trusted your word alone. Lord Jesus, you took our infirmities and bore our diseases; heal the sick we bring to you today, and raise us up to serve you. Amen.
altar: Before Communion we repeat the centurion's words, changing only one: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. The roof is now our own heart, and the Guest is the Lord himself, who comes to us in his Body and Blood. Like Abraham at Mamre we do not prepare a feast for God; at the altar God prepares the feast for us.

quick: Abraham runs to welcome three strangers at Mamre, and in them the Lord himself visits him.
Sarah laughs at the promise of a son; the Lord asks: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
A Gentile centurion trusts Jesus' word alone, and Jesus heals his servant, Peter's mother-in-law and many sick.
2027-06-26.action: Welcome someone into your home this week with simple hospitality.
2027-06-26.question: Do I trust that Jesus' word is enough, or do I always need to see before I believe?

family.explain: Abraham was sitting outside his tent on a very hot day. He saw three visitors and he ran to meet them! He gave them water to wash their feet, fresh bread, meat and milk, and he stood beside them like a servant. Abraham did not know it yet, but God was visiting him. When we welcome guests kindly, we welcome God too.
family.intention: We pray for travellers, for migrant workers far from home, and for families who welcome guests.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can our family invite for a meal, or help with a kind welcome, this month?”

illus: In many old Syrian Christian and Hindu homes of Kerala there was a custom: a kindi of water stood at the front step so that any visitor could wash his feet before entering, and no one who came at mealtime was sent away without rice. A grandmother in Thrissur used to say to her grandchildren: never ask who it is before you put the water out; you do not know whom God is sending. One monsoon evening a drenched young priest, newly posted to the parish and lost on the way, knocked at that door. He was welcomed, fed and dried before anyone knew who he was. Years later, at her funeral, he preached on Genesis 18. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you visited Abraham at Mamre. Visit us now, and make us a people who welcome you in every guest. Amen.
share: He ran from the tent entrance to meet them (Genesis 18:2). How do I receive unexpected guests, at home, in the parish, in my plans?
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? (Genesis 18:14). In which situation of my life do I need to hear this question today?
Only speak the word, and my servant will be healed (Matthew 8:8). Whom am I carrying to Jesus in prayer, as the centurion carried his servant?
pm.resp: The Lord has remembered his mercy.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a house of welcome for strangers, migrants and the poor.
For families who are waiting for a child, and for all who wait for a promise of God that seems impossible.
For soldiers, police officers and all who hold authority, that they may use it with humility and faith like the centurion.
For the sick of our parish, and for those who serve them as Peter's mother-in-law served the Lord.
For our group, that through the prayers of Mary we may believe that nothing is impossible with God.
pm.close: Father, you remembered your promise to Abraham and fulfilled it in Christ. Welcome us at your table with all the nations. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, picture the scene. It is the hottest part of the day. Old Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent. He looks up and sees three strangers. And this man of ninety-nine years runs to meet them, bows down, brings water for their feet, has bread baked and a calf prepared, and stands beside them like a servant while they eat (Genesis 18:1–8). He does not know who they are. But the Bible tells us: the Lord appeared to Abraham. When he welcomed strangers, he welcomed God.

Then the visitor says: your wife Sarah shall have a son. Sarah is listening behind the tent, and she laughs to herself. I am old, my husband is old. And the Lord asks: why did Sarah laugh? Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? (Genesis 18:14). That is the question of today. Is anything too wonderful for him? Is your family situation too difficult? Is your sin too great? Is your sorrow too deep? Nothing is too wonderful for the Lord.

Centuries later an angel said the same thing to a young girl in Nazareth: nothing will be impossible with God. Sarah laughed and hid. Mary believed, and sang the song we prayed today as our psalm: the Mighty One has done great things for me. On this Saturday let us ask Mary to teach us her faith.

And in the Gospel a Roman officer shows us that faith can be found where we least expect it. Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word (Matthew 8:8). We say his words at every Mass. Let us say them today with his faith, carrying to Jesus the people we love. His word is enough. Amen.
kids: Children, one very hot day Abraham saw three visitors coming. He ran to meet them, gave them water and bread and a big meal. Guess who was visiting? God himself! Then God said: Sarah, you will have a baby. Sarah laughed, because she was very old. But God said: is anything too hard for the Lord? No! Nothing is too hard for God. And when visitors come to your house, be kind and share, like Abraham!

intro: Theme: “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?”
Hospitality at Mamre, a promise that makes Sarah laugh and Mary sing, and a soldier whose faith amazes Jesus.

q: He said, “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.
points.apply: This week offer simple hospitality to someone who is not family: a meal, a cup of tea, a place to rest.

points.h: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
q: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? At the set time I will return to you, in due season, and Sarah shall have a son.
For nothing will be impossible with God.
points.apply: Write down the situation you find most impossible, and pray over it each evening this week with the Magnificat.

sub: Many will come from east and west.
q: He sent out his word and healed them, and delivered them from destruction.
The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.
points.apply: Before each Communion this week, name silently one person you bring to the Lord with the centurion's words.

concl: At Mamre God comes as a guest and asks Sarah, and us, whether anything is too wonderful for him.
Mary's faith and the centurion's faith show the answer: God's word is enough, and his table is open to all nations.
2027-06-26.resolve: Welcome one guest this week as if Christ himself had come to your door.
